explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says, "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free," and then he tells them, "Stand firm" (Galatians 5:1). He is not telling them to go find freedom somewhere else. He is telling them to stay put in the freedom Christ already gave.

explanations.answer: Work hard to earn their freedom
explanations.explanation: Not this one, friend. Paul does not say to earn freedom. He says Christ has already set them free, and because of that they are to "stand firm" (Galatians 5:1). The verse starts with Christ's work, not theirs.

That is not Paul's point here. He tells them to "stand firm" and not be encumbered again by a yoke of slavery (Galatians 5:1). This is about holding fast to freedom, not going silent. Paul sounds like a man planting his feet.

That's right. Paul says, "Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1). He is warning them not to get tangled up again in bondage. Freedom is theirs in Christ, so he tells them to stay there.

The verse really says the opposite. Paul warns them, "do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1). So yes, he absolutely is warning them not to be weighed down again. He sees that danger and says it plain.

You got it. Paul says, "if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all" (Galatians 5:2). That is a sharp warning. He wants them to see that trusting in that path empties Christ's value for them.

No, friend. Paul does not say Christ will become more valuable. He says, "if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all" (Galatians 5:2). That line lands hard for a reason.

Not here. Paul is not saying nothing changes. He says Christ "will be of no value to you at all" if they let themselves be circumcised in this way (Galatians 5:2). Paul is drawing a line, not shrugging his shoulders.

This one came out underbaked. Paul says the man who gets himself circumcised "is obligated to obey the whole law" (Galatians 5:3). Not one command. The whole thing. That's a load nobody should pretend is small.

Correct. Paul says such a man "is obligated to obey the whole law" (Galatians 5:3). He does not get to pick one part and leave the rest on the tray. Paul is showing how total that obligation would be.

explanations.answer: They have been severed from Christ
explanations.explanation: Yes. Paul says to those trying to be justified by the law, "you have been severed from Christ; you have fallen away from grace" (Galatians 5:4). That is why this passage feels so urgent. He is not treating this like a tiny side issue.

explanations.answer: They have drawn closer to Christ
explanations.explanation: No, baker. Paul says the opposite. Those trying to be justified by the law "have been severed from Christ" and "have fallen away from grace" (Galatians 5:4). He sees this as separation, not nearness.

Not at all. Paul does not say they gained more grace. He says, "you have fallen away from grace" when they try to be justified by the law (Galatians 5:4). Whew. Paul opens the oven door and the heat comes right out.
Fine work, baker. Paul says, "by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness" (Galatians 5:5). Faith is the way he names it here. Not law. Not grinding effort. Faith.

That is not the word Paul uses. He says, "by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness" (Galatians 5:5). This whole section is pushing against confidence in the law as the way of being justified. So when Paul fills in the blank, he writes faith.

No, friend. Paul does not say they eagerly await through effort. He says it is "by faith" and "through the Spirit" that they await the hope of righteousness (Galatians 5:5). Human strain is not the engine in this verse.

That's a keeper. Paul says, "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value. What matters is faith expressing itself through love" (Galatians 5:6). There it is, clean and clear. What matters is not that outward mark but faith working through love.

Not this one. Verse 6 does not say perfect command-keeping is what matters here. It says, "What matters is faith expressing itself through love" (Galatians 5:6). Paul keeps bringing them back to faith, not law-keeping as the ground.

explanations.answer: Coming from the right family line
explanations.explanation: Nope. Paul does not point to ancestry here. He says neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has value in Christ Jesus, and then says, "What matters is faith expressing itself through love" (Galatians 5:6). He aims at what is true in Christ, not family status.
This one is still doughy. Paul says, "Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you" (Galatians 5:8). So he is not crediting that persuasion to God. He is ruling that idea out.

Right answer. Paul says plainly, "Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you" (Galatians 5:8). Whatever is pulling them off course, Paul says it is not from the One who called them. Short verse. Strong point.
Perfect bake. Paul says, "A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough" (Galatians 5:9). Not part of it. The whole batch. That is why even a little false persuasion matters.
Not according to Paul. He does not say leaven stays near the surface. He says it works through "the whole batch of dough" (Galatians 5:9). Small thing, big spread. That is the warning.
No, friend. Paul's picture is bigger than that. He says a little leaven works through "the whole batch of dough" (Galatians 5:9). It does not stay politely in one corner. It moves through everything.

Yes. Paul says, "The one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be" (Galatians 5:10). Paul is confident in the Lord about the Galatians, and he is just as clear that the troubler will answer for it. He leaves no wiggle room there.

explanations.answer: He will be let off free
explanations.explanation: No, baker. Paul says the exact opposite. The one troubling them "will bear the judgment, whoever he may be" (Galatians 5:10). Paul does not wave this away like nothing happened.

explanations.answer: He will be put in charge
explanations.explanation: Not this one. Paul is not promoting the troubler. He says, "The one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be" (Galatians 5:10). That line is warning, not reward.

Came out burnt, friend. Paul is not admitting that he still preaches circumcision. He asks, "if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?" (Galatians 5:11). The question pushes the other way. His persecution shows that is not what he is preaching.

Exactly. Paul asks that question to make a point, not a confession: "if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?" (Galatians 5:11). Then he adds, "In that case the offense of the cross has been abolished" (Galatians 5:11). He is showing that he is not preaching that message.

Baked just right. Paul says, "you were called to freedom," and then warns, "do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh" (Galatians 5:13). Freedom is real, but it is not a license for the flesh. Paul guards both truths at once.

The verse really does warn them. Paul says, "do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh" (Galatians 5:13). So the statement is true. He wants their freedom to move toward loving service, not toward the flesh.
Box-worthy. Paul says, "The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: 'Love your neighbor as yourself'" (Galatians 5:14). He gives that line as the summary here. One sentence, and it reaches wide.

That is a command from Scripture, but it is not the one Paul quotes here. In this verse he says, "The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: 'Love your neighbor as yourself'" (Galatians 5:14). So that is the line to hold onto in this passage.

Not this time. Paul does not quote that command in Galatians 5:14. He says the entire law is fulfilled in, "Love your neighbor as yourself" (Galatians 5:14). That is the decree he puts front and center.

You got it, baker. Paul warns, "if you keep on biting and devouring one another, watch out, or you will be consumed by one another" (Galatians 5:15). He is showing where that kind of behavior leads. It eats a group alive.

That is not the word Paul uses. He says they will be "consumed by one another" if they keep on biting and devouring one another (Galatians 5:15). The warning is fierce because the damage is fierce. People can tear each other down fast.

No, friend. Paul's word is "consumed," not shamed (Galatians 5:15). He warns, "if you keep on biting and devouring one another, watch out, or you will be consumed by one another" (Galatians 5:15). He is talking about destructive conflict turning back on the whole group.
